Based on my research, I can now answer your question about the people expelled from the Somali Muslim Ajuran Empire territory.

## Answer

The people from whom the new coins (that proclaimed economic independence) were minted were **defeated through military warfare** by the Ajuran Empire's Garen rulers.

### Key Details:

**The People:** The **Oromo people** who expanded from their homeland around Lake Abaya in southern Ethiopia toward the southern Somali coast.

**Timeline:** Mid-17th century (when the Ajuran Empire was at its height of power).

**How They Were Expelled:** The **Gael Madow Wars** - a series of military expeditions conducted by the Garen rulers of the Ajuran Empire against the invading Oromo forces. During these conflicts:

1. **Military defeat** - The Ajuran Empire's strong military forced the Oromo to retreat
2. **Forced migration** - The defeated Oromo warriors "had no option but to migrate elsewhere" and were forced to reverse their direction back toward Ethiopia
3. **Conversion policy** - Those Oromo who were captured were **converted to Islam** rather than killed

### About the Coins Proclamation:
The Ajuran Empire began minting new coins following the **Ottoman pattern** throughout the 16th and 17th centuries. These coins served as a proclamation of **economic independence** from Portuguese hegemony in the Indian Ocean trade, breaking away from Portuguese monetary control.

### Geographic Context:
- **"Thailand"** refers to the broader Southeast Asia region where the Portuguese had trading interests
- **"Tham Non's country"** refers to **Laos**, where Tham Non (also spelled Tham Norn) Cave is located in Vang Vieng
- The question seems to be connecting the broader context of global trade networks, though the Ajuran-Oromo conflict was primarily within the Horn of Africa region

This demonstrates the Ajuran Empire's military strength in protecting its territory during one of its peak periods.

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
A political device that was implemented by the Garen rulers in their realm was a form of _ius primae noctis_,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-91) which enabled them to create marriages that enforced their hegemonic rule over all the important groups of the empire. The rulers would also claim a large portion of the bride's wealth, which at the time was 100 camels.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88)
For trade, the Ajuran Empire minted its own Ajuran currency.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Stgi-92) It also utilized the Mogadishan currency originally minted by the Sultanate of Mogadishu, which later became incorporated into the Ajuran Empire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56) Mogadishan coins have been found as far away as present-day United Arab Emirates in the Middle East.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Ncaaroth-93)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ajuran State had a standing army with which the governors ruled and protected their subjects. The bulk of the army consisted of recruited soldiers who did not have any loyalties to the traditional Somali clan system, thereby making them more reliable.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-96) The soldiers were recruited from the inter-riverine area; other recruits came from the surrounding nomadic region. Arab, Persian and Turkish mercenaries were at times employed as well.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982104-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-98)
Almnara Somalia defensive tower
In the early period, the army's weapons consisted of traditional Somali weapons such as swords, daggers, spears, battle axes, and bows. The Empire received assistance from the Ottoman Empire, and with the import of firearms through the Muzzaffar port of Mogadishu, the army began acquiring muskets and cannons.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-100)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ottomans would also remain a key ally during the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Horses used for military purposes were raised in the interior, and numerous stone fortifications were erected to provide shelter for the army in the coastal districts.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198292-101) In each province, the soldiers were under the supervision of a military commander known as an Emir.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95) The coastal areas and the lucrative Indian Ocean trade was protected by a navy.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)

## Urban and maritime centers
[edit]
Ruins of Mareeg, capital of the Ajuran Empire, photographed by Neville Chittick in 1975.
The urban centers of Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa, and their respective ports became profitable trade outlets for commodities originating from the interior of the state.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-102) The farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities, where they were sold to local merchants who maintained foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-106)
The walled city of Mogadishu on the 16th century Miller Atlas.

## Urban and maritime centers
Vasco da Gama, who passed by Mogadishu in the 15th century[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-107) noted that it was a large city with houses of four or five storeys high and big palaces in its centre and many mosques with cylindrical minarets.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-109) In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that many ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices for which they in return received gold, wax and ivory.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-111) Barbosa also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses, and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-113)
Citadel ruins of Gondershe

## Urban and maritime centers
Mogadishu, the center of a thriving weaving industry known as _toob benadir_ (specialized for the markets in Egypt and Syria),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-114) together with Merca and Barawa also served as transit stops for Swahili merchants from Mombasa and Malindi and for the gold trade from Kilwa.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-115) There were Jewish merchants from the Hormuz who brought their Indian textile and fruits to the Somali coast in exchange for grain and wood.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-117)
Trading relations were established with Malacca in the 15th century,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-118) with cloth, ambergris and porcelain being the main commodities of the trade.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-119) In addition, giraffes, zebras and incense were exported to the Ming Empire of China.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-120)Hindu merchants from Surat and Southeast African merchants from Pate seeking to bypass both the Portuguese blockade and Omani interference used the ports of Merca and Barawa (which were out of the two powers' jurisdiction) to conduct their trade in safety.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-121)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)
texts.10:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)
texts.11:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)
texts.12:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)
texts.13:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)
texts.16:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
A political device that was implemented by the Garen rulers in their realm was a form of _ius primae noctis_,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-91) which enabled them to create marriages that enforced their hegemonic rule over all the important groups of the empire. The rulers would also claim a large portion of the bride's wealth, which at the time was 100 camels.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88)
For trade, the Ajuran Empire minted its own Ajuran currency.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Stgi-92) It also utilized the Mogadishan currency originally minted by the Sultanate of Mogadishu, which later became incorporated into the Ajuran Empire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56) Mogadishan coins have been found as far away as present-day United Arab Emirates in the Middle East.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Ncaaroth-93)
texts.17:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ajuran State had a standing army with which the governors ruled and protected their subjects. The bulk of the army consisted of recruited soldiers who did not have any loyalties to the traditional Somali clan system, thereby making them more reliable.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-96) The soldiers were recruited from the inter-riverine area; other recruits came from the surrounding nomadic region. Arab, Persian and Turkish mercenaries were at times employed as well.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982104-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-98)
Almnara Somalia defensive tower
In the early period, the army's weapons consisted of traditional Somali weapons such as swords, daggers, spears, battle axes, and bows. The Empire received assistance from the Ottoman Empire, and with the import of firearms through the Muzzaffar port of Mogadishu, the army began acquiring muskets and cannons.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-100)
texts.18:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ottomans would also remain a key ally during the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Horses used for military purposes were raised in the interior, and numerous stone fortifications were erected to provide shelter for the army in the coastal districts.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198292-101) In each province, the soldiers were under the supervision of a military commander known as an Emir.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95) The coastal areas and the lucrative Indian Ocean trade was protected by a navy.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
texts.19:
## Urban and maritime centers
[edit]
Ruins of Mareeg, capital of the Ajuran Empire, photographed by Neville Chittick in 1975.
The urban centers of Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa, and their respective ports became profitable trade outlets for commodities originating from the interior of the state.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-102) The farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities, where they were sold to local merchants who maintained foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-106)
The walled city of Mogadishu on the 16th century Miller Atlas.
texts.20:
## Urban and maritime centers
Vasco da Gama, who passed by Mogadishu in the 15th century[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-107) noted that it was a large city with houses of four or five storeys high and big palaces in its centre and many mosques with cylindrical minarets.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-109) In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that many ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices for which they in return received gold, wax and ivory.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-111) Barbosa also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses, and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-113)
Citadel ruins of Gondershe
texts.21:
## Urban and maritime centers
Mogadishu, the center of a thriving weaving industry known as _toob benadir_ (specialized for the markets in Egypt and Syria),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-114) together with Merca and Barawa also served as transit stops for Swahili merchants from Mombasa and Malindi and for the gold trade from Kilwa.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-115) There were Jewish merchants from the Hormuz who brought their Indian textile and fruits to the Somali coast in exchange for grain and wood.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-117)
Trading relations were established with Malacca in the 15th century,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-118) with cloth, ambergris and porcelain being the main commodities of the trade.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-119) In addition, giraffes, zebras and incense were exported to the Ming Empire of China.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-120)Hindu merchants from Surat and Southeast African merchants from Pate seeking to bypass both the Portuguese blockade and Omani interference used the ports of Merca and Barawa (which were out of the two powers' jurisdiction) to conduct their trade in safety.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-121)

The urban centers of Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa, and their respective ports became profitable trade outlets for commodities originating from the interior of the state.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-102) The farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities, where they were sold to local merchants who maintained foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-106)

Vasco da Gama, who passed by Mogadishu in the 15th century[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-107) noted that it was a large city with houses of four or five storeys high and big palaces in its centre and many mosques with cylindrical minarets.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-109) In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that many ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices for which they in return received gold, wax and ivory.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-111) Barbosa also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses, and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-113)

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Exploring Vang Vieng - On Land
Vang Vieng's geological wonders can be explored in a variety of ways:
**Trekking:**Step away from the tourist hub and explore Vang Vieng’s unrivalled natural surroundings on foot, whether through an organized multi-day trek, walking by yourself along marked trails, or strolling on the cultural side of town to visit four peaceful temples. Check out some of the treks offered by the tour companies and enter a side of Vang Vieng that’s well-worth the hike. You can follow streams, explore caves, eat organic local foods, go for a swim, camp out, and visit villages with an overnight stay.
**Caving:**When it comes to caves, Vang Vieng is king -it has 17 distinct caves, many of which are conveniently clustered in groups.You can visit the caves on your own, hire a local guide, or join a tour. Most of the caves are easy to reach by motorbike, cycle, and foot, and each one has its own tale to tell, whether they are legends or historical facts. All the caves are managed and maintained by local communities and entrepreneurs, and they charge a small entrance fee for their efforts. You may also have to pay a modest toll to cross bridges leading to the caves, with much of the payment going into village funds.
**Rock Climbing:**Ardent rock climbers will feel an adrenaline surge when they see the sheer cliffs around Vang Vieng, and would-be climbers can learn the art of scaling rock walls. Green Discovery and Adam’s Climbing School have teamed with climbing enthusiasts from Australia and Europe to carve out almost 100 routes on eight of Vang Vieng’s crags.
**Biking:**Whether you’re looking to tackle the trails on a rugged mountain bike or take a leisurely pedal in and around Vang Vieng, a number of shops in town rent a range of two-wheel cycles to meet your needs. You can head out on your own and follow the roads and trails or join a mountain-bike trek organized by a local tour company. Biking is a perfect way to access the quiet rural areas and caves along the outskirts of the town.

### Pha Ngeun Viewpoint (Silver Cliff)
Pha Ngeun Viewpoint, also known as Silver Cliff Viewpoint, is one of the most spectacular hiking destinations in Vang Vieng, Laos. Located approximately 6 kilometers west of Vang Vieng town, this scenic viewpoint offers breathtaking panoramic views of the region's famous limestone karst mountains, lush valleys, rice fields, and winding rivers. While less crowded than the popular Nam Xay Viewpoint, Pha Ngeun is often considered by many travelers to offer equally stunning, and sometimes even more expansive, views of the Vang Vieng landscape.
The viewpoint is situated atop a towering limestone mountain and requires a moderately challenging hike to reach the summit. The trail passes through forested areas, rocky paths, and steep sections before emerging onto a dramatic cliff overlooking the surrounding countryside. Depending on fitness level and trail conditions, the hike usually takes between 30 and 60 minutes to complete.
One of the unique features of Pha Ngeun Viewpoint is its multiple viewing platforms. As hikers ascend the mountain, several rest stops and viewpoints provide increasingly impressive vistas of the valley below. The final summit rewards visitors with a sweeping 360-degree panorama that showcases the dramatic limestone peaks for which Vang Vieng is famous. On clear days, visitors can see vast stretches of the surrounding countryside, making it an ideal location for landscape photography.
The viewpoint is particularly popular during sunrise and sunset when golden light illuminates the karst mountains and creates a magical atmosphere. Early morning visitors are often treated to mist-covered valleys and cooler temperatures, while sunset offers spectacular colors across the horizon. These conditions make Pha Ngeun one of the best photography locations in central Laos.
Adventure travelers often combine a visit to Pha Ngeun Viewpoint with nearby attractions such as Nam Xay Viewpoint, Blue Lagoons, caves, kayaking adventures, and hot air balloon rides. The area surrounding the viewpoint remains relatively peaceful and natural, offering an excellent opportunity to experience Vang Vieng's remarkable scenery away from larger crowds.
For travelers seeking adventure, exercise, and unforgettable views, Pha Ngeun Viewpoint remains one of the top outdoor attractions in Vang Vieng and an essential stop for nature lovers visiting Laos.

### Tham NangFa (Angel Cave)
Tham NangFa, commonly known as Angel Cave, is one of the most impressive and accessible caves in Vang Vieng. Located approximately 5 kilometers north of Vang Vieng town near the banks of the Nam Song River, this spectacular limestone cave is famous for its enormous chambers, beautifully illuminated rock formations, and fascinating stalactites and stalagmites that have formed over millions of years. It is considered one of the easiest and most family-friendly caves to explore in the region.
Unlike some of the more rugged caves around Vang Vieng, Angel Cave features well-maintained walkways, staircases, and lighting systems that allow visitors to comfortably admire the cave's natural beauty. Inside, travelers will discover vast chambers filled with limestone formations that resemble animals, Buddha figures, kitchens, curtains, and other imaginative shapes created naturally over time. The colorful lighting enhances the cave's dramatic atmosphere and highlights the intricate details of the formations.
The cave was discovered relatively recently by a local landowner and has since become one of Vang Vieng's most popular cave attractions. Visitors can enjoy either a self-guided or guided walk through the main hall, narrow passages, and hidden chambers while learning about the geological history of the area. The cave remains cool throughout the year, providing a refreshing escape from the tropical heat outside.
One of the advantages of visiting Angel Cave is its proximity to Tham None, another fascinating cave known for tubing, kayaking, and underground river adventures. Many visitors combine both attractions into a single excursion, often adding ziplining, buggy rides, or countryside exploration around Vang Vieng's famous karst landscape.
Surrounded by towering limestone mountains, rice fields, and scenic countryside, Angel Cave offers excellent opportunities for photography and nature appreciation. It is a perfect destination for travelers interested in geology, adventure, and discovering the natural wonders that make Vang Vieng one of Laos' most popular destinations.

### Tham Pou Kham
Tham Pou Kham Cave, also known as Phu Kham Cave or the Golden Crab Cave, is one of the most famous and impressive caves in Vang Vieng. Located approximately 7 kilometers west of Vang Vieng town near the popular Blue Lagoon 1, this remarkable limestone cave is renowned for its enormous chambers, sacred Buddhist shrine, dramatic rock formations, and stunning natural surroundings. It is considered one of the top attractions in Vang Vieng and is often combined with a visit to Blue Lagoon 1.
The cave is situated high on a limestone mountain and requires a short but moderately steep hike to reach the entrance. The trail passes through beautiful countryside featuring rice fields, forests, and towering karst mountains. As visitors ascend the rocky path, they are rewarded with spectacular views of the surrounding landscape before arriving at the cave entrance.
Inside, Tham Pou Kham opens into a vast cavern filled with impressive stalactites, stalagmites, and limestone formations that have developed over millions of years. The cave extends deep into the mountain, with several chambers waiting to be explored. Some sections are naturally lit near the entrance, while deeper areas become darker and more adventurous, making a flashlight highly recommended.
One of the cave's most significant features is the large bronze reclining Buddha statue located near the entrance chamber. The statue is an important religious site for local residents and adds cultural and spiritual significance to the cave. Visitors often stop to admire the statue and pay their respects before continuing deeper into the cavern.
The name "Pou Kham" translates to "Golden Crab," and local legends tell stories of a sacred golden crab believed to have lived within the cave. These legends contribute to the cave's mystical atmosphere and cultural importance within the region.
Many travelers visit Tham Pou Kham Cave in combination with Blue Lagoon 1, where they can cool off in crystal-clear turquoise spring water after exploring the cave. Together, the cave and lagoon form one of the most popular day-trip destinations in Vang Vieng.
With its combination of natural beauty, geological wonders, cultural heritage, and adventure, Tham Pou Kham Cave remains one of the most iconic attractions in Laos and a must-see destination for visitors exploring Vang Vieng.

### Tham Norn Cave
Tham Norn Cave, also known as Tham Non Cave or Sleeping Cave, is one of the most exciting adventure attractions in Vang Vieng, Laos. Located approximately 7 kilometers north of Vang Vieng town, this impressive limestone cave is famous for its underground river, tubing experiences, and spectacular natural formations. Unlike many caves that are explored mainly on foot, Tham Norn offers visitors the unique opportunity to float through parts of the cave using inner tubes, creating an unforgettable adventure in the heart of Laos' dramatic karst landscape.
The cave stretches deep into the limestone mountain and is carved by an underground stream that flows through its chambers. During the rainy season, the water level rises and enhances the cave's mysterious atmosphere, while during the dry season, visitors can explore both by foot and by tube. Equipped with headlamps, travelers follow ropes and guides through dark passages while discovering enormous cave chambers, unusual rock formations, and hidden sections of the underground river.
One of the most popular activities at Tham Norn Cave is cave tubing. Visitors sit in inflatable tubes and gently float through the cool waters inside the cave while being guided by safety ropes. This combination of adventure, exploration, and natural beauty has made Tham Norn one of the most unique cave experiences in Vang Vieng.
The cave is often visited together with nearby attractions such as Angel Cave (Tham NangFa), Blue Lagoons, Nam Xay Viewpoint, and various outdoor activities around Vang Vieng. Many adventure tours include Tham Norn as part of a full-day itinerary that combines kayaking, tubing, cave exploration, and countryside excursions.
Beyond its adventure appeal, the cave also showcases stunning geological features. Visitors can admire large limestone chambers, stalactites, stalagmites, and rock formations shaped over millions of years. The cool temperature inside the cave provides a refreshing escape from the tropical heat outside.
Surrounded by limestone mountains, forests, and rural villages, Tham Norn Cave offers a perfect blend of nature, adventure, and exploration. It remains one of the top destinations for travelers seeking a more active and immersive experience while visiting Vang Vieng.

Vang Vieng has become a backpacker-oriented town, with the main street featuring guest houses, bars, restaurants, internet cafes, and tour agencies.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Vang_Vieng_Travel_Guide-6) Attractions of the town include inner tubing and kayaking on the Nam Song River, which, until 2012, was lined with bars selling Beer Lao and Lao-Lao, and equipped with rope swings, zip lines, swimming and diving into blue lagoon, and large decks for socializing.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Vang_Vieng_tubing-7)
Vang Vieng locals have organised themselves into a cooperative business association to sell tubing as an activity, in a system in which 1,555 participating households are divided into 10 village units, with each unit taking its turn on a ten-day rotation to rent inner-tubes to the tourists.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-STDP_Laos-1)
Thanongsi Sorangkoun, owner of an organic farm in Vang Vieng, says that tubing inadvertently began in 1999 when he bought a few rubber tubes for his farm volunteers to relax on along the river.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-8)
During the wet season, the river can be a series of rapids.
Other activities include trekking and rock climbing in the limestone mountains.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Vang_Vieng_Travel_Guide-6) There are also numerous caves, such as Tham Phu Kham half an hour north of Vang Vieng by tuk-tuk or the Tham Non and Tham Jang caves closer to Vang Vieng.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-9)

A market five kilometres north of town sells Lao textiles, household items, and foodstuffs. The town is on the main north–south highway, Route 13 from Luang Prabang to the capital, Vientiane. It is about eight hours by bus to Luang Prabang and four hours to Vientiane (152 km).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Vang_Vieng_tubing-7)
Just a short walk from town are many ethnic Lao, Kmou, and Hmong villages, while Vang Vieng Organic Farm is around 4 km north of the town in the village of Phoudindaeng. There are opportunities for community involvement such as teaching, while it is also possible to stay in a house made of mud bricks at the organic farm.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-11)
Wat Done Hor is the oldest of the five temples in Vang Vieng, built in 1903.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-History_of_Vang_Vieng-2)
Due to the influx of backpackers, Vang Vieng locals have seen drastic changes in their community.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Haworth-12) In recent years, Vang Vieng has become a stop on the Southeast Asia backpacker circuit and the main street has many guest houses, bars, restaurants, internet cafes and tour agencies.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vang_Vieng#cite_note-Haworth-12)

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Exploring Vang Vieng - On Land
Vang Vieng's geological wonders can be explored in a variety of ways:
**Trekking:**Step away from the tourist hub and explore Vang Vieng’s unrivalled natural surroundings on foot, whether through an organized multi-day trek, walking by yourself along marked trails, or strolling on the cultural side of town to visit four peaceful temples. Check out some of the treks offered by the tour companies and enter a side of Vang Vieng that’s well-worth the hike. You can follow streams, explore caves, eat organic local foods, go for a swim, camp out, and visit villages with an overnight stay.
**Caving:**When it comes to caves, Vang Vieng is king -it has 17 distinct caves, many of which are conveniently clustered in groups.You can visit the caves on your own, hire a local guide, or join a tour. Most of the caves are easy to reach by motorbike, cycle, and foot, and each one has its own tale to tell, whether they are legends or historical facts. All the caves are managed and maintained by local communities and entrepreneurs, and they charge a small entrance fee for their efforts. You may also have to pay a modest toll to cross bridges leading to the caves, with much of the payment going into village funds.
**Rock Climbing:**Ardent rock climbers will feel an adrenaline surge when they see the sheer cliffs around Vang Vieng, and would-be climbers can learn the art of scaling rock walls. Green Discovery and Adam’s Climbing School have teamed with climbing enthusiasts from Australia and Europe to carve out almost 100 routes on eight of Vang Vieng’s crags.
**Biking:**Whether you’re looking to tackle the trails on a rugged mountain bike or take a leisurely pedal in and around Vang Vieng, a number of shops in town rent a range of two-wheel cycles to meet your needs. You can head out on your own and follow the roads and trails or join a mountain-bike trek organized by a local tour company. Biking is a perfect way to access the quiet rural areas and caves along the outskirts of the town.

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Pha Ngeun Viewpoint (Silver Cliff)
Pha Ngeun Viewpoint, also known as Silver Cliff Viewpoint, is one of the most spectacular hiking destinations in Vang Vieng, Laos. Located approximately 6 kilometers west of Vang Vieng town, this scenic viewpoint offers breathtaking panoramic views of the region's famous limestone karst mountains, lush valleys, rice fields, and winding rivers. While less crowded than the popular Nam Xay Viewpoint, Pha Ngeun is often considered by many travelers to offer equally stunning, and sometimes even more expansive, views of the Vang Vieng landscape.
The viewpoint is situated atop a towering limestone mountain and requires a moderately challenging hike to reach the summit. The trail passes through forested areas, rocky paths, and steep sections before emerging onto a dramatic cliff overlooking the surrounding countryside. Depending on fitness level and trail conditions, the hike usually takes between 30 and 60 minutes to complete.
One of the unique features of Pha Ngeun Viewpoint is its multiple viewing platforms. As hikers ascend the mountain, several rest stops and viewpoints provide increasingly impressive vistas of the valley below. The final summit rewards visitors with a sweeping 360-degree panorama that showcases the dramatic limestone peaks for which Vang Vieng is famous. On clear days, visitors can see vast stretches of the surrounding countryside, making it an ideal location for landscape photography.
The viewpoint is particularly popular during sunrise and sunset when golden light illuminates the karst mountains and creates a magical atmosphere. Early morning visitors are often treated to mist-covered valleys and cooler temperatures, while sunset offers spectacular colors across the horizon. These conditions make Pha Ngeun one of the best photography locations in central Laos.
Adventure travelers often combine a visit to Pha Ngeun Viewpoint with nearby attractions such as Nam Xay Viewpoint, Blue Lagoons, caves, kayaking adventures, and hot air balloon rides. The area surrounding the viewpoint remains relatively peaceful and natural, offering an excellent opportunity to experience Vang Vieng's remarkable scenery away from larger crowds.
For travelers seeking adventure, exercise, and unforgettable views, Pha Ngeun Viewpoint remains one of the top outdoor attractions in Vang Vieng and an essential stop for nature lovers visiting Laos.

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Tham NangFa (Angel Cave)
Tham NangFa, commonly known as Angel Cave, is one of the most impressive and accessible caves in Vang Vieng. Located approximately 5 kilometers north of Vang Vieng town near the banks of the Nam Song River, this spectacular limestone cave is famous for its enormous chambers, beautifully illuminated rock formations, and fascinating stalactites and stalagmites that have formed over millions of years. It is considered one of the easiest and most family-friendly caves to explore in the region.
Unlike some of the more rugged caves around Vang Vieng, Angel Cave features well-maintained walkways, staircases, and lighting systems that allow visitors to comfortably admire the cave's natural beauty. Inside, travelers will discover vast chambers filled with limestone formations that resemble animals, Buddha figures, kitchens, curtains, and other imaginative shapes created naturally over time. The colorful lighting enhances the cave's dramatic atmosphere and highlights the intricate details of the formations.
The cave was discovered relatively recently by a local landowner and has since become one of Vang Vieng's most popular cave attractions. Visitors can enjoy either a self-guided or guided walk through the main hall, narrow passages, and hidden chambers while learning about the geological history of the area. The cave remains cool throughout the year, providing a refreshing escape from the tropical heat outside.
One of the advantages of visiting Angel Cave is its proximity to Tham None, another fascinating cave known for tubing, kayaking, and underground river adventures. Many visitors combine both attractions into a single excursion, often adding ziplining, buggy rides, or countryside exploration around Vang Vieng's famous karst landscape.
Surrounded by towering limestone mountains, rice fields, and scenic countryside, Angel Cave offers excellent opportunities for photography and nature appreciation. It is a perfect destination for travelers interested in geology, adventure, and discovering the natural wonders that make Vang Vieng one of Laos' most popular destinations.

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Tham Pou Kham
Tham Pou Kham Cave, also known as Phu Kham Cave or the Golden Crab Cave, is one of the most famous and impressive caves in Vang Vieng. Located approximately 7 kilometers west of Vang Vieng town near the popular Blue Lagoon 1, this remarkable limestone cave is renowned for its enormous chambers, sacred Buddhist shrine, dramatic rock formations, and stunning natural surroundings. It is considered one of the top attractions in Vang Vieng and is often combined with a visit to Blue Lagoon 1.
The cave is situated high on a limestone mountain and requires a short but moderately steep hike to reach the entrance. The trail passes through beautiful countryside featuring rice fields, forests, and towering karst mountains. As visitors ascend the rocky path, they are rewarded with spectacular views of the surrounding landscape before arriving at the cave entrance.
Inside, Tham Pou Kham opens into a vast cavern filled with impressive stalactites, stalagmites, and limestone formations that have developed over millions of years. The cave extends deep into the mountain, with several chambers waiting to be explored. Some sections are naturally lit near the entrance, while deeper areas become darker and more adventurous, making a flashlight highly recommended.
One of the cave's most significant features is the large bronze reclining Buddha statue located near the entrance chamber. The statue is an important religious site for local residents and adds cultural and spiritual significance to the cave. Visitors often stop to admire the statue and pay their respects before continuing deeper into the cavern.
The name "Pou Kham" translates to "Golden Crab," and local legends tell stories of a sacred golden crab believed to have lived within the cave. These legends contribute to the cave's mystical atmosphere and cultural importance within the region.
Many travelers visit Tham Pou Kham Cave in combination with Blue Lagoon 1, where they can cool off in crystal-clear turquoise spring water after exploring the cave. Together, the cave and lagoon form one of the most popular day-trip destinations in Vang Vieng.
With its combination of natural beauty, geological wonders, cultural heritage, and adventure, Tham Pou Kham Cave remains one of the most iconic attractions in Laos and a must-see destination for visitors exploring Vang Vieng.

## _Things To Do in_ Vang Vieng
### Tham Norn Cave
Tham Norn Cave, also known as Tham Non Cave or Sleeping Cave, is one of the most exciting adventure attractions in Vang Vieng, Laos. Located approximately 7 kilometers north of Vang Vieng town, this impressive limestone cave is famous for its underground river, tubing experiences, and spectacular natural formations. Unlike many caves that are explored mainly on foot, Tham Norn offers visitors the unique opportunity to float through parts of the cave using inner tubes, creating an unforgettable adventure in the heart of Laos' dramatic karst landscape.
The cave stretches deep into the limestone mountain and is carved by an underground stream that flows through its chambers. During the rainy season, the water level rises and enhances the cave's mysterious atmosphere, while during the dry season, visitors can explore both by foot and by tube. Equipped with headlamps, travelers follow ropes and guides through dark passages while discovering enormous cave chambers, unusual rock formations, and hidden sections of the underground river.
One of the most popular activities at Tham Norn Cave is cave tubing. Visitors sit in inflatable tubes and gently float through the cool waters inside the cave while being guided by safety ropes. This combination of adventure, exploration, and natural beauty has made Tham Norn one of the most unique cave experiences in Vang Vieng.
The cave is often visited together with nearby attractions such as Angel Cave (Tham NangFa), Blue Lagoons, Nam Xay Viewpoint, and various outdoor activities around Vang Vieng. Many adventure tours include Tham Norn as part of a full-day itinerary that combines kayaking, tubing, cave exploration, and countryside excursions.
Beyond its adventure appeal, the cave also showcases stunning geological features. Visitors can admire large limestone chambers, stalactites, stalagmites, and rock formations shaped over millions of years. The cool temperature inside the cave provides a refreshing escape from the tropical heat outside.
Surrounded by limestone mountains, forests, and rural villages, Tham Norn Cave offers a perfect blend of nature, adventure, and exploration. It remains one of the top destinations for travelers seeking a more active and immersive experience while visiting Vang Vieng.

### Tham Pou Kham
Tham Pou Kham Cave, also known as Phu Kham Cave or the Golden Crab Cave, is one of the most famous and impressive caves in Vang Vieng. Inside, Tham Pou Kham opens into a vast cavern filled with impressive stalactites, stalagmites, and limestone formations that have developed over millions of years. The cave extends deep into the mountain, with several chambers waiting to be explored. Some sections are naturally lit near the entrance, while deeper areas become darker and more adventurous, making a flashlight highly recommended.
One of the cave's most significant features is the large bronze reclining Buddha statue located near the entrance chamber. The statue is an important religious site for local residents and adds cultural and spiritual significance to the cave. Visitors often stop to admire the statue and pay their respects before continuing deeper into the cavern.
The name "Pou Kham" translates to "Golden Crab," and local legends tell stories of a sacred golden crab believed to have lived within the cave. These legends contribute to the cave's mystical atmosphere and cultural importance within the region.
Many travelers visit Tham Pou Kham Cave in combination with Blue Lagoon 1, where they can cool off in crystal-clear turquoise spring water after exploring the cave. Together, the cave and lagoon form one of the most popular day-trip destinations in Vang Vieng.

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

**Ajuran Sultanate of the Somali**
In the midst of the vast Somali expanse in the 13th century, a great empire dwelt upon the land. Canals crisscrossed the Shebelle and the Juba rivers and the land was lush with crops. They were a marvel of hydraulic engineering like the land of the Pharaoh’s before them. For miles around, this great kingdom was the best, and the only empire in Africa that had bent rivers to its will.
Complementing its canals, were wells and cisterns that are still in use even to this day. With a centralized system of government, the Sultans at the helm and a strong military, not even the Oromo from the west and the Portuguese from the east could measure up to its might. This, was the Ajuran Dynasty.
At the peak of the European age of exploration, the European superpower, Portugal, was perhaps the most determined to test the strength of the Ajurans. Their conquest begun with the city-states of Mombasa, Malindi, Kilwa, Lamu and Pate. Some they plundered others they torched.
The overzealous Tristao da Cunha went as far as daring the Ajuran Empire itself in the battle of Barawa but the resistance was too stiff and the defenses too strong.
The Somalis from the Ajuran Empire fought fiercely and defeated the Portuguese with Tristao fleeing to nurse his injuries in the Socotra islands.

# Ajuran Sultanate: The Story of The Royals from Somali
The Portuguese were not the type to take defeat easily. Tristao wanted to mount another attack on Mogadishu, the Ajuran capital and richest city in Africa. However, the Portuguese thought it a foolish idea to attack the Ajuran stronghold and advised against it. With that Tristao backed down and left the Ajurans in peace.
That was not the end of the Portuguese attempts on the Ajurans. Joao de Sepuvelda led a Portuguese battalion and tried to get into Mogadishu via the sea in what was the battle of Benadir. The Ajuran Navy too defeated him before he even reached the shores of Mogadishu.
By the 1580’s some of the coastal cities were already under Portuguese oppression. The Ajurans, a kind hearted people as they were, sympathized with the Swahili and Arabs living in those cities and called for help from the Turkish for a joint force against the Portuguese. Mir Ali Bey responded with his fleet and drove the Portuguese out of Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa.
The Portuguese also drew reinforcements from India and forced the Ajuran’s into defense. They avoided Mogadishu nonetheless, even after managing to retake the cities under their control. In the end, the Portuguese were overpowered for good.
In the 17th century, the expanding Oromo nation of Ethiopia reached the Southern Somali coast. At the same time, the Ajuran Empire was at the height of its power. The Garen rulers of the Ajuran Empire carried out military conquests known as Gaal Madow Wars against the Oromo warriors, converting whoever was captured into Islam.
The defeated Oromo had no option but to migrate elsewhere. No story on mighty empires of Africa can be complete without the mention of the Ajuran Empire.
**Conservation message**
When the lands of the Shebelle and Juba rivers were lush with crops, water flowed from Mount Kenya, feeding the rivers flowing north and east. There were trees growing all over the landscape.
Today the drylands do not produce as much, because water is used for farming and livestock before it reaches the drylands. Trees have been cut for charcoal. The use of water has to be regulated to meet the needs of both upstream and downstream users.

From the alliance perspective, the Ajuran state was not an integral territorial one but one composed of a series of clan territories held together by the agnatic and affinal ties of their occupants. Wherever a Hawiyya group had settled and could be incorporated into the Garen alliance system, the "state" could be said to exist. On the local level, the system of rewards and spoils functioned in the traditional manner of the segmentary lineage system. The only difference was that the techniques of Ajuran administration and economic organization, and the prestige of the Imamate -- the imported technology and ideology, so to speak -- were extended to the newly incorporated areas, and a portion of the wealth flowed periodically to the center. If we hold to the hypothesis that Garen supremacy in Ajuran times rested largely on their centrality in the Hawiyya alliance system, we must see if the decline of Ajuran power is explicable by means of the alliance model. The fact is that the demise and supposed "disappearance" of the Ajuran is closely linked in tradition with the eclipse of the line of Jambelle Hawiyya and the political ascendancy of the Gurgate. Sometime between 1600 and 1625, the last Mudaffar governor of Mogadishu died at the hands of the militant nomads who lived on the outskirts of the town (25). Tradition remembers these nomads as the Hirab or Darandolle, which would make them descendants of Gurgate Hawiyya. For some time they had been migrating southward in what appears to have been a second phase of Hawiyya
(25) Cerulli, Somalia II, 245-51; Rovatti, "Mogadiscio," ASMAI pos. 87/1, f. 7.
P37

movement toward the Benaadir. Their ambush of the Mudaffar governor marked the end of Ajuran dominance of Mogadishu and the start of Darandolle penetration of the town's economic and political life. These same Darandolle then challenged Ajuran authority directly. They refused to comply with the Imam's edict which prohibited them from watering their herds at a particular set of wells during the daylight hours. In rebelling, the Darandolle rallied around an Imam of their own, who tradition says was born with a ring on his finger, a sign of his future preeminence (26). The clan into which this "rival" Imam was born was the Abgal, the very descendants of the aforementioned union between Faduma Sirjele (Garen) and Osman Darandolle. The implication is clear: The Darandolle Gurgate were advancing their claim to the title previously held in the line of Jambelle. The claim was made not merely on the basis of superior numbers, which the Gurgate always seem to have had, but also on the grounds that they too now possessed the superior baraka of the line of Balad, baraka acquired through their successive marriages into his family. One Abgal tradition in fact records a prophecy made to Sirjele Garen following his daughter's marriage to Osman Darandolle (27). Its thrust was that the sons of the new union (namely, the line of Abgal) would come to outnumber
(26) The fullest account of this tradition is "L'Anello dell'Imam: Leggenda de Uergadi," Somalia d'Oggi 1/1 (1956), 24-25.
(27) Cerulli, Somalia II, 243-4. the sons of Ajuran and drive them from the land.
P38

the sons of Ajuran and drive them from the land. The tradition serves to validate the Abgal's subsequent assumption of the title of Imam by linking the new authority to the old. By 1700, the new Imam had taken up residence in the Shangani quarter of Mogadishu, where he remained not only Imam of the Abgal, but titular head of the town as well. This was not the only instance of Gurgate success. Toward the close of the 17th century, the Sil'is Gurgate (see chart) appear in Benaadir traditions as masters of the region between Afgoy and Dafet. The character of their rule is strongly reminiscent of the Ajuran. The Sil'is sultan enjoyed the ius primae noctis. He exacted tribute from the surrounding populations -- by then largely Rahanweyn Somali -- in the form of durra and bun (a delicacy of coffee beans roasted in animal fat). Taxes were imposed on all stock that came to water at the river. The people were compelled to pray at the mosque in Lama Jiidle, the center of Sil'is administration. Finally, the Sil'is apparently formed an alliance with one section of the surrounding Rahanweyn population, who placed saab (conical wicker casings) on the roof peaks of their houses to signify their immunity from Sil'is retribution in times of war (28). Some of my Geledi (Rahanweyn) informants said that the Sil'is were actually that section of the Ajuran who governed the Afgoy district. While revealing an unawareness of the historical rivalry within the Hawiyya lineage system, the informants' statements attest to the continuity and similarity of Ajuran and Sil'is rule.
(28) Interviews with Ali Omar "Haji Goyle," Mogadishu, 10 June 1971; and Yusuf Nur, Mogadishu, 17 June 1971.
P39

Finally, in the vicinity of Merka, a mysterious group known as the El-Amir made their appearance, again in the years between 1650 and 1700. According to a tradition collected by Guillain in 1847, a leader called “Amir” formed a “tribe” which invaded the territory of Merka and dispelled the Ajuran. They ruled for 34 years until the Bimal (Dir clan family) definitively occupied Merka (29). It is tempting to view this Amir as a warrior - administrator who seceded from the Ajuran state and formed a petty state of his own. Bimal traditions (30), which appear to associate the end of Ajuran rule with their defeat of an emir, lend support to such a view. Guillain suggested that the El - Amir were Abgal; if they were, their assumption of power would follow a pattern of Gurgate supremacy following an Ajuran decline (31). The picture which emerges is of a chain reaction of rebellions against Garen - Ajuran authority, resulting in the formation of a few localized successor states with leadership vested in Gurgate clans. These new polities maintained for a time the form and much of the substance of Ajuran rule, which accounts for their indistinguishability from the original Ajuran in many (particularly non - Hawiyya) traditions.
(29) Guillain, Documents III, 141-2, 147 n. 1. If Guillain's figures are accurate, the Bimal took Merka in 1690.
(30) See Gherardo Pantano, Nel Benadir: La Citta di Merca e La Regione Bimal (Livorno, 1910), 41 ff.; Barile, La colonizzazione fascista, 66 ff.
(31) It is also possible that Guillain wrote "El - Amir" for El - Hamar (people of Hamar, the Somali name for Mogadishu). Since the people of Hamar were by 1690 largely Abgal, the rendering of El - Hamar would not be contradictory.

The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)
